solution:
Given: plate 10 cm \(\times\) 0.5 cm \(\times\) 0.2 cm, \(H = 0.5 \times 10^{4}\) A m\(^{-1}\), induced magnetic moment \(m = 0.5\) A m\(^{2}\). Take \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T m A\(^{-1}\).

Step 1 - volume of the plate.
\(V = (10 \times 10^{-2})(0.5 \times 10^{-2})(0.2 \times 10^{-2}) = 1 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^{3}\).

Step 2 - magnetisation. By Eq. (11.12), magnetisation is magnetic moment per unit volume:
\(M = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{0.5}{1 \times 10^{-6}} = 5 \times 10^{5}\) A m\(^{-1}\).

Step 3 - magnetic induction. By Eq. (11.15),
\(B = \mu_{0}(H + M) = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (0.5 \times 10^{4} + 5 \times 10^{5})\)
\(B = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5.05 \times 10^{5} = 0.6346\) T.

\(\therefore\) the magnetic induction in the plate is \(B \approx 0.635\) Wb m\(^{-2}\) (T).

Note that the magnetising field \(H\) contributes only 1 % of the bracket here; dropping it would give 0.628 T, so it must be kept.

Given: Moment of Inertia \(I = 500\) g cm\(^2\)
Frequency \(n = 10\) oscillation per minute \(= 10/60\) oscillations per second
Time period \(T = 6\) sec
\(B_{H} = 0.36\) gauss
From Eq. (11.8),
\(m = \dfrac{4\pi^2 I}{T^2 B}\)
\(m = \dfrac{4 \times (3.14)^2 \times 500 \times 10^{-7}}{36 \times 0.36 \times 10^{-4}}\)
\(m = 1.522\) A m\(^2\)
note: The substitution with pi = 3.14 gives 1.5215 A m^2, printed 1.524.

solution:
[Textbook misprint: the stem describes a **toroidal** ring wound on a straight rod of length \( 1 \) m and diameter \( 1 \) cm, which is not a coherent geometry: a toroid closes on itself and has no length in that sense. The stem is preserved as printed. The answer is unaffected either way: read as a solenoid of length \( 1 \) m, or as a toroid of mean circumference \( 1 \) m, both give \( B = \mu_0 n i \) and \( L = \mu_0 n^2 l A \) with the same numbers.]

First convert the turn density and find the cross-sectional area.

\(n = 100\ \text{turns/cm} = 100 \times 100 = 1 \times 10^{4}\) turns/m

With \(l = 1\) m, the total number of turns is \(N = n l = 1 \times 10^{4}\).

Diameter \(= 1\ \text{cm}\), so radius \(r = 0.5\ \text{cm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-2}\) m and

\(A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (0.5 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 7.854 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2\)

**Magnetic field inside the bar**

\(B = \mu_0 n i = (4\pi \times 10^{-7})(1 \times 10^{4})(1)\)

\(B = 1.257 \times 10^{-2}\) T

**Self-inductance of the coil**

\(L = \dfrac{N\phi}{i} = \dfrac{N B A}{i} = \mu_0 n^2 l A\)

\(L = (4\pi \times 10^{-7})(1 \times 10^{4})^2 (1)(7.854 \times 10^{-5})\)

\(L = 9.870 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{H} = 9.870\) mH

The permeability of the rod is stated to be that of free space, so no relative permeability \(\mu_{\mathrm{r}}\) factor enters; had the core been ferromagnetic, \(L\) would have been larger by that factor. Note also that \(L \propto n^2\), so the turns density enters **squared**, once through the field it produces and once through the number of turns that field links.

Given: \(n = 1500\) turns/m, \(i = 3.0\) A, coil C has \(A = 25\ \text{cm}^2 = 25 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\) and \(N_{\mathrm{c}} = 150\) turns, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T.m/A, reversal time \(\mathrm{d}t = 0.5\) s.

**(a) Magnetic flux density at the centre of the solenoid**

\(B = \mu_0 n i = (4\pi \times 10^{-7})(1500)(3.0)\)

\(B = 5.65 \times 10^{-3}\) T

**(b) Flux linkage in coil C**

Coil C is wound tightly round the centre of the solenoid, so the whole of \(B\) threads each of its turns:

\(N_{\mathrm{c}}\phi = N_{\mathrm{c}} B A = 150 \times (5.65 \times 10^{-3}) \times (25 \times 10^{-4})\)

\(N_{\mathrm{c}}\phi = 2.12 \times 10^{-3}\) Wb

**(c) Average emf induced in coil C on reversing the current**

This is the step where marks are usually lost. Reversing the current does not take the flux linkage to zero; it takes it to \(-2.12 \times 10^{-3}\) Wb. The **change** is therefore twice the value found in (b):

\(|\Delta (N_{\mathrm{c}}\phi)| = 2 \times 2.12 \times 10^{-3} = 4.24 \times 10^{-3}\) Wb

\(|e|_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{|\Delta (N_{\mathrm{c}}\phi)|}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{4.24 \times 10^{-3}}{0.5}\)

\(|e|_{\text{avg}} = 8.48 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V} = 8.48\) mV

Had the current merely been switched off instead of reversed, the answer would have been half of this, \(4.24 \times 10^{-3}\) V.
note: 4 pi x 1500 x 3 x 1e-7 = 5.655e-3 -> 5.65e-3 T (printed 5.66); later figures unchanged.

solution:
[Textbook misprint: the question asks for the flux cut **per second**, but the printed key gives part (b) as \( 1.130 \) Wb. The unit must be Wb s\( ^{-1} \): a flux cut per second is a rate, and the same numeral read as a plain flux would contradict the question's own wording. The magnitude is correct; only the unit is misprinted.]

Given: \(f = 20\) rev/s, \(R = 30\ \text{cm} = 0.30\) m, \(B = 0.20\) T, with \(\vec{B}\) parallel to the axis of rotation and therefore **perpendicular to the plane of the disc**.

**(a) Area swept out per second by the radius**

In one complete revolution the radius sweeps out the whole area of the disc, \(\pi R^2\). It makes \(f\) revolutions each second, so

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = \pi R^2 f = 3.142 \times (0.30)^2 \times 20\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = 5.656\ \text{m}^2\) per second

**(b) Flux cut per second by the radius**

Since \(\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to the plane, the flux cut per second is just \(B\) times the area swept per second:

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = B \dfrac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0.20 \times 5.656\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = 1.131\ \text{Wb}\) per second

**(c) Induced emf in the disc**

By Faraday's law the magnitude of the emf equals the flux cut per second:

\(|e| = \left| \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} \right| = 1.131\) V

This is why (b) and (c) come out as the same number in different units: a weber per second **is** a volt. As a cross-check, this is the Faraday-disc result \(e = \tfrac{1}{2}B\omega R^2\) with \(\omega = 2\pi f = 125.7\) rad/s, which gives \(\tfrac{1}{2}(0.20)(125.7)(0.09) = 1.131\) V, agreeing to the rounding in \(\pi\).

The emf appears between the **rim and the centre** of the disc, and it is steady rather than alternating.
note: 0.20 x 5.656 = 1.1312, printed 1.130 in (b) and (c); the note's quote of the book key is left as it is.

solution:
The wire AB (\(l = 10\) cm) is moving to the right with the tangential velocity v.

\(\left| \vec{\mathrm{v}} \right| = \left| \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r} \right|\)

v \(= \omega r\) where \(\omega\) is angular velocity and \(r\) is the radius.

\(\mathrm{v} = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} \cdot r\)  \(\left[ \because \omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} \right]\)

\(= 2\pi \nu r\)

\(= 2\pi \cdot \left( \dfrac{1500}{60\,\mathrm{s}} \right) \cdot \left( \dfrac{4}{100} \right) \mathrm{m}\)  \(\left[ \because r = AD = (4/100)\,\mathrm{m} \right]\)

\(= 2\pi\) m/s

\(= 6.283\) m/s

The magnetic field is directed vertically upward from North to South pole. As the wire AB is cutting the magnetic lines of force perpendicularly, the induced emf is, therefore, maximum.

\(\because e = Bl\mathrm{v} \sin\theta\) with \(\theta = 90^\circ\),

Then, \(e = e_{\max} = Bl\mathrm{v}\)

\(= (0.5\ \text{N/A.m})\,(10/100)\,\text{m} \cdot (6.28\ \text{m/s})\)

\(= \dfrac{0.5}{10} \times 6.28\)

\(= 0.314\) V

or \(e_{\max} \approx 314.2\) mV.

The emf induced in the wires BC and DA is zero because the magnetic Lorentz force on free electrons in these wire \(\left[ \vec{F} = q(\vec{\mathrm{v}} \times \vec{B}) \right]\) has no component parallel to the wires. Also there is no e.m.f. in the lead in wires, which are stationary and are not in motion \((\vec{\mathrm{v}} = 0)\). Therefore the total emf between the terminals P and Q is due the movement of segment AB. i.e., \(e = 314\) mV. The direction of induced emf is given by Lenz's law.

The magnetic flux through each turn of area \(A\) in the solenoid is

\(\phi_B = B \cdot A = (\mu_0 n i) \cdot A\)  \((\because\) Magnetic field inside a solenoid is \(B = \mu_0 ni)\)

\(= \mu_0 (N/l) \cdot i \cdot A\)  \((\because n\) is the number of turns per unit length \(= N/l)\)

We know that the inductance \((L)\) of the solenoid can be written as

\(L = (N \phi_B)/i\)

Substituting the value of \(\phi_B\), we get

\(L = (N/i) \cdot \{ \mu_0 \cdot (N/l) \cdot i \cdot A \}\)

\(L = \mu_0 \cdot (N^2/l) \cdot A\)

Inserting the given values of \(N\), \(l\) and \(A\), we find

\(L = (4\pi \cdot 10^{-7}\,\text{Tm}/A) \cdot (200)^2 (5 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2)/(20 \cdot 10^{-2}\,\text{m})\)

or \(L \approx 0.1257\) mH

The induced emf in the solenoid

\(e_{\mathrm{L}} = -L\,(\mathrm{d}i/\mathrm{d}t)\)

\(e_{\mathrm{L}} = -(0.1257 \cdot 10^{-3})\,(-60\ \text{A/s}) = 7.54\) mV
note: l = 20 cm is 20e-2 m (printed 20e-4); e = 0.1257e-3 x 60 = 7.54 mV (printed 0.126e-3 and 7.543).

solution:
The magnetic field inside a toroid,

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N i}{2\pi r_0}\), where \(N\) is the number of turns and \(r_0\) is the distance from the toroidal axis. If \(r << R\), we can use \(r_0 \cong R\). Hence,

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N i}{2\,u\,R}\)

The magnetic flux \((\phi)\) passing through cavity is

\(\phi = \left( \pi r^2 \right) \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi} \dfrac{Ni}{R} = \dfrac{\mu_0 N i r^2}{2R}\)

This is the flux that links each turn. When the current \(i\) varies with time, the induced emf \(e\) across the terminals of toroid is given by Faraday's law.

\(e = -\dfrac{N \mathrm{d}\phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = -N \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 N i r^2}{2R} \right)\)

\(e = -N \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 N r^2}{2R} \right) \dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

Comparing with \(e = -L \dfrac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\)

We get,

\(L = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2} \dfrac{N^2 r^2}{R}\)   \((\because r << R)\)

Given,

\(N = 1200\), \(r = 2.0\) cm, \(R = 15\) cm and \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T.m/A.

\(L = 2.413 \times 10^{-3}\) H

Given
\(\lambda_{uv} = 3000\, \mathring{A} = 3000 \times 10^{-10}\) m,
\(\lambda_{red} = 7000\, \mathring{A} = 7000 \times 10^{-10}\) m and
\(\nu_{FM} = 98.3\) MHz \(= 98.3 \times 10^{6}\) s\(^{-1}\)

We know that energy \(E\) of electromagnetic radiation of frequency \(\nu\) is \(h\nu\) and if \(\lambda\) is the corresponding wavelength, then \(\lambda\nu = c\), \(c\) being the speed of electromagnetic radiation in vacuum.

Hence, \(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)

(a)
\(E = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s} \times 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}}{3000 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}}\)
\(= 6.63 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 4.144\) eV
for a photon corresponding to ultraviolet light and

\(E = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s} \times 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}}{7000 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}}\)
\(= 2.84 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 1.776\) eV
for a photon corresponding to red light.

(b) The energy of photon of FM frequency 98.3 MHz is \(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\) J s \(\times\ 98.3 \times 10^{6}\) s\(^{-1}\)
\(= 651.73 \times 10^{-28}\) J \(= 40.73 \times 10^{-8}\) eV.

This is very small energy as compared to the photon energy in the visible range.

Given
Intensity of radiation \(= 0.5 \times 10^{-4}\) W/m\(^2\),
Area of cathode \(= 5\) cm\(^2 = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\).
Radius of potassium atom \(= 230\) pm \(= 230 \times 10^{-12}\) m
Work function of potassium \(= 2.3\) eV \(= 2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J

The number \(N\) of electrons present on the surface of cathode can be approximately calculated assuming that each potassium atom contributes one electron and the radius of potassium atom is \(230 \times 10^{-12}\) m.

\(N =\) Area of cathode / area covered by one atom
\(= 5 \times 10^{-4} / (3.1415 \times 230 \times 10^{-12} \times 230 \times 10^{-12})\)
\(= 3009 \times 10^{12}\)

Incident power on the cathode is
\(= 0.5 \times 10^{-4}\) W/m\(^2 \times 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\)
\(= 2.5 \times 10^{-8}\) W

Wave theory assumes that this power distributed over the whole area of the cathode is uniformly absorbed by all the electrons. Therefore the energy absorbed by each electron in one second is
\(= 2.5 \times 10^{-8}\) W \(/\, 3009 \times 10^{12} \approx 8.308 \times 10^{-24}\) W.

Work function of potassium is
\(2.30\) eV \(= 2.30 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(= 3.68 \times 10^{-19}\) J.

Hence each electron will require minimum \(3.68 \times 10^{-19}\) J of energy to be knocked off from the surface of the cathode.

The time required to accumulate this energy will be
\(3.68 \times 10^{-19}\) J \(/\, 8.31 \times 10^{-24}\) W
\(= 4.428 \times 10^{4}\) s, which is about half a day.
